vignette:
The Weight He Carries

Rajan is a 36-year-old South Asian man who works as a detective in a mid-sized urban police department. He has been married for eight years to a woman he describes as patient and kind, though he adds this last part quietly, as though he doesn't quite understand why she stays. He comes to sessions in plain clothes, never his badge, and sits with his back to the wall.

He grew up in a household that looked ordinary from the outside. His father was a respected man in their community — well-dressed, well-spoken, present at every temple function. Behind closed doors, he was something else entirely. From the time Rajan was approximately five years old until he left for university at eighteen, his father beat him with regularity and without predictability. A missed chore, a wrong tone of voice, a school mark that fell short of expectation — any of these could trigger an eruption. What Rajan remembers most is not any single incident but the permanent state of waiting: scanning his father's face the moment he walked through the door, reading the set of his jaw, the pace of his footsteps, calibrating the atmosphere of the room before he had even put down his bag.

He left home and did not look back. He became a detective, he says, because he is good at reading people — at noticing what doesn't fit, at anticipating danger before it arrives. He has never connected this skill to what it cost him to develop it. He speaks about his professional life with genuine pride. He has closed difficult cases. His colleagues trust him. He is, by most measures, very good at his job.

But the past does not stay in the past. Rajan wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, the details of old memories sharp and unwelcome. He rarely remembers a specific dream, only the feeling — that the walls are too close, that something is about to happen. He lies still in the dark and runs through the house in his mind, checking doors, checking his wife's breathing, checking that everything is as it should be. He does not go back to sleep.

At work, he finds himself hypervigilant in ways that sometimes serve him and sometimes do not. He is easily startled by raised voices in the precinct. When a senior officer dresses him down in front of colleagues — even mildly, even fairly — something in him goes cold and distant, and he cannot access the words he wants. He describes this as going somewhere else. Afterward he is flooded with shame, though he cannot always say why.

His marriage carries the strain of all of this. He is not physically present in the way his wife needs. When she reaches for him after a nightmare, he goes rigid. He does not want to be touched when his body is still in that other place. He knows this hurts her. He has tried to explain it and found that he has no language that feels adequate. What he wants her to understand is that it is not about her, but the explanation feels thin even to him.

He does not drink. He does not lose his temper at home. He is, in many ways, a man who has worked very hard to be nothing like his father, and he has largely succeeded. But success has come at a cost. He is exhausted by the vigilance, worn down by years of monitoring every room he enters and every face he reads. He describes feeling fundamentally different from other people — as though something in him was set wrong early and has never quite corrected itself.

He agreed to come to therapy, he says, because his wife asked him to. He is not sure he believes it will help. But he is here, back against the wall, watching the door.
